drafts.walkScript: People admire Mr Darcy at first, 'till his manners gave a disgust' on line 31. That means the way he acted put people off him. Line 32 says he was 'proud' and 'above his company'. He acted as if he were better than everyone there. Being angry that the ball closed early is Mr Bingley, at line 37.

Look at Mr Bingley's speech on lines 51 and 52. It says 'I must have you dance' and ends 'You had much better dance'. Both parts push his friend towards the dancing. The words 'stupid manner' describe standing about alone, not anything said about the ladies.

Lines 70 and 71 say she was left with 'no very cordial feelings' towards Mr Darcy. So she has not forgiven him and is not pleased with him. Yet line 71 says she told the story 'with great spirit'. Lines 72 and 73 say she 'delighted in anything ridiculous'. She turns his rudeness into something to laugh at.

Line 7 gives the rule: 'Named things went in the first box to be returned.' At lines 13 and 14 he keeps it, even for a girl who has left. Lines 31 and 32 show he knows it is his; line 46 shows it is named. Yet line 33 puts it in 'the Friday box', so the rule bends for him alone.

Line 38 says the sheet is for 'September football trials'. Line 39 adds that there is 'plenty of room left at the bottom'. At line 37 Reuben only passes it, on his way to fetch a bin bag. Nothing says he adds his name. The empty room is a place he could take and does not.

At line 47 his reason is 'It won't fit me next year.' Line 48 says she looked 'a second or two longer than the answer needed'. That longer look shows she is not sure his reason is the real one. Yet at line 49 she folds it 'the way he had folded it'. She leaves it in the box, so she lets his reason stand.

Line 7 says named things went in the first box 'to be returned'. Lines 8 and 9 say the other box was going to 'the charity collection'. At line 13 the cardigan's owner 'had left in Year Four'. Line 14 says he put it in the returns box 'anyway'. He knew she had gone, yet chose returning over giving it to charity.

Line 41 says they set the kettle on the fire 'at about half-past five'. Line 39 says Mother found them 'deeply asleep' at eight o'clock. So for two and a half hours, nobody took the kettle off the fire. Line 42 says 'the water had all boiled away'. With no water left, the bottom burned out of the kettle.

Line 24 says the narrator could hear 'how much water' there was. Lines 25 and 26 say it was 'higher up than the field' beside the path. Line 18 says the wall is 'only a bank of earth'. Water piled up above the land, held back by earth, is an uneasy sight. So line 26 says the narrator 'did not look over for a while'.
